title: Anthony Butler, United States chargé d'affaires in Mexico, private letter partly in "my private Cypher" (55 code numbers and 4 signs among plain English)
correspondents: Anthony Butler → addressee not established (the endorsement's second line is an abbreviation, read "To J. S. M—"; Narváez 2019 names Charles Th. O'Gorman)
shelfmark: NARA RG 59, Despatches from United States Ministers to Mexico, microfilm M97, roll 6 ("Volume 5", National Archives Catalog item 189100166), frame 233
folio_note: frame 233: one leaf, two pages, "Mexico 30 October 1830", "Dear Sir", unsigned; code numbers from the second paragraph on, standing among plain words: 55 numbers (54 whole, one cut off in the film's gutter), 43 different values from 1 to 614, separated by full stops, and 4 signs (an open triangle, a blotted triangle, an X, a small flourish). Endorsed below the text "Mr Butler / To J. S. M— / my private Cypher" (the initials doubtful)
status: Seen on the frame image (21 Nov 2026), transcribed twice, the second time blind. No decipherment over the numbers or in the margins; none on frames 230-232 and 234-236, and the catalog's page text of the whole roll has no other page in this number style. Not in the State Department code of the period in which 1385 = the: a test written before it was run failed both parts (no number above 660, against 65% in Butler's 1834 letters in that code; 0 of 3 context probes). Weber (1979) cites the letter for the words "my private cypher" and guesses a nomenclator; Narváez (2019, p. 131 and nn. 45-46) says the cipher passages have no clear text in the archive's copy. Not found on DECODE; not in the repository (known.py).
why: The only text known to us in the private cipher of Jackson's agent in Mexico, written while he was negotiating the treaty of commerce; its plain words speak of "sharp sparring" and of matters in doubt.
score_note: Scored from the frame image during the Nov 2026 search of Anthony Butler's papers on NARA M97 (research/sweep_2026-11-22_ajbeling_mexico/); viewed
verify: Open Bosch García, Documentos de la relación de México con los Estados Unidos, vol. II (UNAM 1983), at 30 Oct 1830 (its host did not answer on 22 Nov 2026); look for more text in the same cipher among Butler's private letters of 1829-31 (Van Buren and Jackson papers, Library of Congress); open frames 214-229 and 237-247 of roll 6 as images.

title: F. J. Lobo, Mexican consul at Clifton, Arizona → Ignacio Bonillas, Washington: cipher telegram that Bonillas could not read (with a second of 26 Nov)
correspondents: F. J. Lobo, Mexican consul at Clifton, Arizona → Ignacio Bonillas, Mexican embassy, Washington
shelfmark: Archivo Histórico Genaro Estrada, Secretaría de Relaciones Exteriores (AHGE-SRE), Archivo de la Embajada de México en Estados Unidos (AEMEUA), leg. 507, exp. 6, unfoliated
folio_note: Two telegrams, of 25 and 26 Nov, and Bonillas's oficio A-743 of 27 Nov asking Lobo whether his office held the "Murciélago" key. The 25 Nov telegram is pictured in Narváez 2019, p. 344, fig. 14: a Western Union form received in Washington, three typed lines of five-letter groups, the word "OCHO", the signature "F J LOBO", a handwritten word below it and pencil marks over some groups. The 26 Nov telegram is not pictured.
status: Known only from Narváez 2019, pp. 344-345, nn. 48-49: Bonillas could not decipher the telegrams of 25 and 26 Nov and wrote to Lobo (A-743, 27 Nov); Narváez did not find Lobo's answer; the "Murciélago" square (printed in the book, fig. 8, p. 335) fails on the pictured telegram although "cajista", word 8 of the list, appears on it; Narváez suggests Lobo used a differently arranged square. The caption of fig. 14 gives 1916; p. 345 says Bonillas was writing to Lobo about the key in November 1917. The pencil marks on the form are not identified as a decipherment. Ciphertext seen only as the book's printed figure, in a photograph of a library copy; not transcribed. Not found on DECODE; not in the repository (known.py).
why: A consular telegram of the Carranza government in the United States that its own embassy could not read; it would show how the consulates used the "Murciélago" square.
score_note: Scored from the printed figure and text of Narváez 2019 during the Nov 2026 reading of that book (research/sweep_2026-11-22_ajbeling_mexico/); viewed only in print
verify: Ask AHGE-SRE for images of AEMEUA leg. 507 exp. 6 (both telegrams, A-743 and any answer or decipherment) and settle the year; test the "Murciélago" square of fig. 8 in other arrangements, with the April telegram on pp. 341-343 (figs. 12-13, with its plain text) as a control.
